lessons.title: CLI execution and web boundaries
lessons.summary: Change Ready to Changed, save the file, and run php main.php again. What should this simple CLI script print?
explanation: The command-line interface, or CLI, runs a PHP source file from a terminal. Save the complete example as main.php and run php main.php with a local PHP installation.
<?php begins PHP code. A file containing only PHP normally omits the closing tag so accidental trailing text is not sent as output.

This course verifies PHP 8.5.12 CLI examples. A terminal run does not demonstrate browser-cookie behavior, deployed server headers or connections to an external production database. Local session storage and in-memory database tests are separate capabilities when their extensions are installed.
Running php main.php reads the current file in this ordinary CLI workflow. It is not the separate manual compilation workflow used in C. The app itself does not run PHP.

Complete local PHP example; the app itself does not execute it:
```php
<?php
echo "Ready\n";

```
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Run the file twice with a changed message. Distinguish terminal output from an HTTP response. You may trace it without a PHP interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Dynamic types and explicit inspection
lessons.summary: Replace 7 with "7". What type name prints?
explanation: PHP values can be integers, floating-point numbers, strings, booleans, null and other types. A normal variable name can later hold a value of another type.

get_debug_type($value) returns a readable type name. This function call receives a value and returns text describing its type. Commas in echo send the listed pieces to output in order; the second piece here is a newline.
7 is an integer; "7" is a string containing a digit. A value looking numeric does not make its stored type an integer.
Expected output or behavior: int. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Strict equality and coercion
lessons.summary: Change === to == in this exact numeric comparison. What prints?
explanation: === is true only when the operands have the same type and equal values. !== is its opposite.
== can compare different types after PHP comparison rules convert them. It is not a general input-validation rule.
var_export($value) prints a PHP-style representation such as true or false. echo prints the following newline separately.
Expected output or behavior: false. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.summary: Change the input to -3.9. What prints?

lessons.title: Boolean values and short-circuit logic
lessons.summary: Replace "0" with "false". What prints?
explanation: In a boolean context, false, null, numeric zero, the empty string, the string "0", and an empty array are false. Other nonempty strings such as "false" are true.
&& evaluates its right side only if the left side is true. || evaluates its right side only if the left side is false.
The explicit (bool) cast shows the conversion in this example. It is not a parser for human words such as yes or false.
Expected output or behavior: false. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.summary: Change the first key from "8" to "08". What count prints?

lessons.title: Array copies and explicit references
lessons.summary: Change $b = $a to $b =& $a. What prints?
explanation: Assigning $b = $a makes changes to ordinary scalar entries in $b independent of $a. PHP can optimize internal storage, but that does not make ordinary assignments aliases.
Writing $b =& $a makes both names refer to the same variable content. This is aliasing, not a deep copy.
The simple example contains only scalar entries. Do not infer that an array assignment recursively clones objects or breaks existing references.
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Match expressions and strict selection
lessons.summary: Change $value to integer 1. What prints?
explanation: match ($value) { pattern => result, default => fallback } chooses a result expression. => connects each matching value with its result.
A match arm uses strict identity rules, so integer 1 and string "1" select different arms unless both are explicitly listed.
A default arm handles otherwise unmatched values. Without one, an unmatched input throws UnhandledMatchError. Arms do not fall through.
Expected output or behavior: other. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Closures and captured values
lessons.summary: Change use ($score) to use (&$score). What prints?
explanation: function (): int { ... } creates a function without declaring a global function name. Assigning it to $read lets $read() call it.
use ($score) captures its current value when the closure is created. A later outer assignment does not replace that captured scalar value.
use (&$score) captures by reference instead, so the closure reads the variable’s later value.

lessons.title: Arrow functions and value capture
lessons.summary: Change only the later assignment from $offset = 9 to $offset = 20. What prints?

Changing $offset afterwards does not replace the captured scalar value. Object values have their own identity rules, taught later.

lessons.title: Exceptions and finally cleanup
lessons.summary: Remove the throw statement. What prints?
explanation: throw new RuntimeException("missing") creates and throws an exception. A catch (RuntimeException $error) block handles that exception type.
Execution jumps out of the try block to the catch. It does not continue with the next ordinary statement inside try.
A finally block runs when control leaves this try/catch normally or through an exception. It does not guarantee cleanup after process termination or a killed process.
TypeError and Exception objects both implement Throwable, but specific catches can be clearer than indiscriminately swallowing all failures.
